Audit prod expense rows for dates that have drifted.
userStories.notes: [P1][Android/Money] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. Already solved on iOS — port, do not redesign. | 2026-08-04 VERIFIED, including the part that makes it embarrassing: the bug is DESCRIBED IN ITS OWN DOC COMMENT and was still shipped. ExpenseDraft.kt:69-71 says outright that re-deriving 'moves an evening expense to the next day east of Greenwich and to the previous day west of it', and :72-73 is exactly that — 'fun isoDate(epochMs: Long, zone: ZoneId = ZoneId.systemDefault()) = Instant.ofEpochMilli(epochMs).atZone(zone).toLocalDate().toString()'. ExpenseRepository.kt:129 calls it inside wireBody. CONFIRMED IT COVERS EDITS, which is the whole premise: wireBody has ONE caller, line 61, on a path that computes 'val id = draft.id ?: UUID.randomUUID()...' with the comment 'An edit keeps its id so the upsert replaces rather than duplicates' and then does client.from(TABLE).upsert(body). One code path for insert and edit, so every re-save re-derives, and the drift compounds per edit rather than settling. So AC3's 'across several edit cycles' is the right test shape. NOTE FOR AC2: iOS solved this at ExpenseStore.swift:34-43 — port that, and check whether the Android ExpenseEntity should carry the calendar date as a string rather than an epoch at all, since as long as the local column is epoch-millis the conversion has to happen somewhere and can be got wrong again.

userStories.title: Android: the local database is reopened per call site and deleted on any open failure
userStories.description: android/.../sync/db/GradeThreadDb.kt:77 — DatabaseProvider.open is not memoized, and line 88 runs context.deleteDatabase(dbName) on any step-1 failure. Four call sites open it: UploadWorker.kt:74, UploadWorker.kt:125, capture/CaptureScreen.kt:76, plus the Hilt singleton. A transient open failure destroys the user's offline data.
acceptanceCriteria: One memoized instance, injected, not opened per call site.
deleteDatabase is reserved for a genuine, identified corruption case and is not the catch-all for any open failure.
Test: a simulated transient open failure does not delete the database.
userStories.notes: [P1][Android/Sync] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. Same class as the iOS SyncEngine finding — silent local data loss. | 2026-08-04 VERIFIED — both ACs hold, but the story's summary is harsher than the code and the correction matters for scoping. THERE IS A RECOVERY LADDER, not a blind delete. DatabaseProvider.open runs three steps: (1) build + force 'db.openHelper.readableDatabase' to make Room's deferred open happen NOW, outcome NORMAL; (2) on ANY step-1 failure, context.deleteDatabase(dbName) + rebuild, outcome RESET; (3) on failure of that, an in-memory database, outcome EPHEMERAL, so it never crashes on data. There is also an outcomeFlow StateFlow feeding a user-facing 'local data was reset' banner. So the user is at least TOLD. THE DEFECT IS STILL REAL and is precisely AC2: step 2 is reached by any step-1 throw — a locked file, a transient I/O error, low storage, a migration hiccup — not only by genuine corruption, and runCatching discards the exception so nothing distinguishes them. AC1 ALSO HOLDS: open() is not memoized, and there are three non-Hilt call sites re-invoking it — CaptureScreen.kt:79 inside a remember, and UploadWorker.kt:74 and :125 — alongside the DatabaseModule.kt:34 Hilt singleton whose own comment (:22) says it is a singleton BECAUSE open runs the recovery. So the singleton's rationale is documented and then bypassed three times, and each bypass is an independent chance to hit the destructive branch. SUGGESTED SHAPE: inject the Hilt-provided instance at all three sites, and gate deleteDatabase on an identified corruption signal (SQLiteDatabaseCorruptException / SQLiteDatabaseLockedException distinction) rather than on Throwable.

Also android/.../platform/net/PlanGate.kt:92 — PlanGateNotifier.gates and .warnings are published to from EdgeApi.kt:54-55 and collected nowhere, so plan-limit messages from the server never reach the user. Wire or delete.
userStories.notes: [P2][Android/Inventory] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | 2026-08-04 VERIFIED, both halves. AC1/AC2: ItemCanvasViewModel.kt's save onSuccess block copies state with saving=false, original=_state.value.draft and savedAtLeastOnce=true — it never clears hasLocalChanges. The flag is set to true at :319 and the ONLY place it is cleared is sync/MutationReplayer.kt:131 (and :142 for sales), on the offline-queue replay path. So a save that succeeds ONLINE never clears it, because the replayer never runs for that mutation. The user is told they have unsaved changes immediately after a successful save, and the sync engine's conflict policy (see the comment at :281) keeps defending a row that has nothing local left to defend — so this is not purely cosmetic, it biases conflict resolution too. AC3 IS A SEPARATE STORY WEARING THIS ONE'S CLOTHES: PlanGateNotifier.gates/.warnings being published to and collected nowhere is a different subsystem, a different fix and a different test. It is fine to leave it here, but do not let it be the reason the dirty-flag fix waits — split it if the flag fix is picked up alone.

userStories.title: The three highest-value money paths have zero tests
userStories.description: services/edge-functions/src/routes/grade.ts is 1,396 lines with no direct tests. routes/admin-billing.ts is 1,756 lines with no tests. lib/affiliate-payout.ts is 500 lines with no tests. grade.ts:1065 fires the refund_snap RPC as `.then(() => {}, () => {})` with both callbacks swallowed. affiliate-payout.ts:209 flips commissions to paid BEFORE the Stripe transfer fires.
acceptanceCriteria: Test coverage for the charge, refund and payout paths in all three files, including the failure branches.
grade.ts:1065's swallowed refund is either handled or explicitly documented as fire-and-forget with a reason.
affiliate-payout.ts:209 marks paid after the transfer succeeds, or uses a two-phase record.

affiliate-payout.ts's SWEEP_LIMIT of 500 (:39) is applied with no .order() on phases b and c, so beyond 500 eligible rows which affiliates get paid is unspecified and possibly permanently starved. Add ordering.
A coverage floor prevents new untested money code.
userStories.notes: [P1][Edge/Tests] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. These three files are where a bug costs real money. | PARTIAL 2026-08-03 — AC2 and AC4 DONE, AC3 ANSWERED (no fix needed, and the story's framing corrected), AC1 and AC5 remain and are scoped below. AC4 WAS THE WORST OF THE THREE and is the reason this was worth taking. The sweep caps each phase at 500 rows. Phase (a) ordered its select; phases (b) and (c) did not. Postgres with no ORDER BY returns an ARBITRARY set — and an arbitrary set from a STABLE PLAN is the SAME 500 rows on every run. So past the cap an affiliate is not delayed, they are permanently starved, and nothing anywhere reports it. Phase (c) is the worse of the two because, unlike the retry phase, it has no age cap to eventually flush a row. Both now order OLDEST FIRST, which is a fairness decision rather than tidiness: a payout failing for a week outranks one that failed a minute ago, and the affiliate who has waited longest gets paid first. The inconsistency WITHIN one function was the tell — phase (a) had the order all along. AC2 DONE. grade.ts refunded a reserved snap with .then(() => {}, () => {}) — both callbacks empty, so a refund that never happened looked exactly like one that did. It stays NON-BLOCKING (the 502 is the honest answer either way, and holding the response on a second database call makes a bad path slower for no benefit), but a failure is now captured. The user is already being told the grade failed; what they must not ALSO get is a silently consumed snap that nobody hears about, because an operator cannot correct a balance nobody recorded as wrong. AC3: TRUE AS WRITTEN, WRONG IN WHAT IT IMPLIES — and no fix applied, which is the part worth reading before someone 'fixes' it later. 'affiliate-payout.ts flips commissions to paid BEFORE the Stripe transfer fires' is literally accurate. But the AC itself offers 'or uses a two-phase record', and that is exactly what this is: affiliate_payouts is the idempotency unit, created pending; claiming commissions into it is what moves them off accrued; the transfer then flips the PAYOUT row to paid or failed. A failed transfer KEEPS the commissions attached so the sweep retries the same idempotency key, and deliberately never releases them — releasing would risk double-paying a transfer that actually went through on a network blip. The code says so in a comment at the failure branch. Reordering this to 'transfer, then mark' would REMOVE a safety property, not add one. THE RESIDUAL HAZARD, which is the useful finding under AC3: the column says 'paid' and means 'claimed into a payout'. Anything summing affiliate_commissions where status='paid' would count money that has not left Stripe. Nothing does today, and a test now fails if something starts to. NEW services/edge-functions/src/tests/money-path-guards_test.ts, 6 cases. The ordering case checks the PROPERTY — a .limit(SWEEP_LIMIT) with no .order() above it — rather than three hand-written phases, so a fourth phase added later is caught; plus a guard-the-guard asserting it still finds three caps, since a rename of SWEEP_LIMIT would otherwise make it pass by finding nothing. The AC3 case pins the four properties that make the two-phase record safe (created pending, claimed into a payout id, an idempotency key on the transfer, failure marking the payout rather than releasing the commissions) — losing any one of them turns the design into the bug the story thought it was. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED THREE WAYS: the create phase's ORDER BY removed, the failure branch made to release commissions, and the refund swallowed again. Each reddened with the right message and was restored. REMAINING AND HONESTLY SCOPED. AC1 asks for coverage of the charge, refund and payout paths in all three files INCLUDING the failure branches. grade.ts (1,396 lines) and admin-billing.ts (1,756) are route files whose handlers need a request context, a Stripe double and a seeded database to drive — that is a test HARNESS, not a test file, and building it is the actual work of AC1. affiliate-payout.ts is the tractable one: its pure decisions already live in affiliate-payout-math.ts and are tested, and what is untested is the IO sequencing, which the dependency-injection shape used for the agent policy engine would suit. AC5 (a coverage floor over money code) is the same job as US-2344 AC3, which asks for an edge coverage floor generally — they should be done together or one will set a floor the other has to move. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1319 files, edge suite 5220 passed / 0 failed. | 2026-08-03 AC5 DONE. AC1 remains and is unchanged in scope. MEASURED BEFORE BUILDING, and the measurement changed the design. The fleet-wide edge floor from US-2344 AC3 cannot see a money file at all: routes/grade.ts and routes/admin-billing.ts are ~3,150 lines that NO test imports, so deno coverage omits them from the table entirely and they contribute nothing to the average. The project number can therefore rise while the three files where a bug costs real money sit at zero — which is exactly the shape AC5 exists to prevent, and a naive per-file floor of 0 would have been decoration on top of it. SO THE FLOOR HAS TWO MECHANISMS, because the files are in two different states. MONEY_FLOORS covers the files that ARE exercised — lib/affiliate-payout.ts at 4.9% line and lib/quick-grade.ts at 12.2%, floored at 4 and 12. Set just below the measurement so they cannot be met by accident: adding untested lines to either drops the percentage and fails. That is 'prevents new untested money code' applied where it can actually bite. MONEY_DEBT is the other half and the more useful one: grade.ts and admin-billing.ts are ENUMERATED as having no coverage rather than silently excluded, and the list is SHRINK-ONLY. The moment a test starts importing either file the script FAILS, demanding it be moved into MONEY_FLOORS in the same commit. Without that, the first test ever written against grade.ts would set no floor, and the coverage it bought could be given straight back — which is how a coverage push quietly evaporates. A THIRD FAILURE MODE WORTH THE CODE: a floored file that VANISHES from the table fails loudly rather than passing. A file nothing imports produces no row, and 'no row' and 'fine' look identical to a naive lookup — so deleting the one test that touches affiliate-payout would otherwise turn the floor green. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED THREE WAYS: a floor raised above the actual (the drop case), a floored file renamed so it disappears from the table, and a debt file given coverage while staying in the debt list. Each exited non-zero with its own message. AC1 UNCHANGED AND STILL HONEST: it asks for coverage of the charge, refund and payout paths INCLUDING failure branches, in all three files. grade.ts and admin-billing.ts need a request context, a Stripe double and a seeded database — a test HARNESS, not a test file, and building it is the actual work. affiliate-payout.ts is the tractable one. The floor above does not substitute for that; it stops the debt growing while it is paid down. A NOTE ON THE TREE: a concurrent agent was editing grading-readiness files during this pass, so only scripts/coverage-floor.mjs and this note were staged. VERIFIED: the floor passes on the current profile (branch 86.3 / function 62.7 / line 49.4 fleet-wide; affiliate-payout 4.9, quick-grade 12.2) and fails on each of the three injected regressions. | 2026-08-03 AC1 DONE FOR affiliate-payout.ts, the file the previous pass called the tractable one. grade.ts and admin-billing.ts remain and their scoping is unchanged. WHAT WAS UNTESTABLE AND WHY. fireTransfer is where the money actually leaves — a Stripe transfer, then a write recording what happened. Its two writes went straight to the service-role client, so exercising the FAILURE branch needed a database, which is why the branch that matters most had no test at all. The writes are injectable now via an optional `io` argument that defaults to exactly what the function did before; the live path is unchanged. SIX BEHAVIOURAL CASES, and the failure branch is the reason for the story: a failed transfer must mark the PAYOUT failed and leave the commissions attached to it, so the sweep retries the SAME idempotency key. Releasing them would risk paying twice for a transfer that actually went through and timed out on the way back. That property is now asserted rather than read. THREE THINGS THE TESTS FOUND WORTH PINNING that a reader would not think to check. (1) A NON-ERROR REJECTION: Stripe's SDK can reject with a plain object, and without the `instanceof Error` fallback the payout would store a null reason — an operator then sees a failed payout with no explanation, which reads as our bug rather than a decline. (2) THE IDEMPOTENCY KEY IS DERIVED FROM THE PAYOUT ID ALONE. Adding anything that varies between attempts — a timestamp, an attempt counter — turns every retry into a second real transfer. (3) BOTH WRITES ARE SCOPED BY AFFILIATE AS WELL AS PAYOUT ID; that second predicate is not redundant, it is what stops a mis-derived payout id marking another affiliate's payout as paid. AN EXISTING GUARD HAD TO FOLLOW THE INDIRECTION, and this is the part I was careful about: money-path-guards_test.ts read the catch block directly for `status: "failed"`, which my refactor moved into the default IO. Weakening it to match would have been the easy move. It now asserts BOTH halves — the catch calls io.markFailed AND the default markFailed writes status:'failed' — because either alone can be satisfied while the property is gone: a markFailed that no longer writes it, or a correct IO that is never called. The release-check runs against both regions too, since a release could now live in either. COVERAGE MOVED AND THE FLOOR MOVED WITH IT: lib/affiliate-payout.ts 4.9% -> 11.6% line, money floor ratcheted 4 -> 11 in the same commit. That is the rule the floor's own header states — raise it alongside the tests that earned it, or the gain can be given straight back. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED SIX WAYS: the failure branch releasing the commissions, the failure branch marking nothing, the indirection kept while the write behind it stops writing 'failed', the idempotency key gaining a timestamp, a write losing its affiliate scoping, and the non-Error fallback removed. Each reddened on its own case. REMAINING: AC1 for routes/grade.ts (~1,400 lines) and routes/admin-billing.ts (~1,750). Both are route files whose handlers need a request context, a Stripe double and a seeded database — a test HARNESS, which is a different piece of work from a test file. They stay declared as MONEY_DEBT in the coverage floor, so the first test written against either fails until it is given a floor. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1336 files, full edge suite 5324 passed / 0 failed, coverage floor green at the new numbers. | 2026-08-03 AC1 ADVANCED for routes/grade.ts — the snap-refund path. The reserved-snap refund lived inline in the handler and called the service-role client directly, which is exactly why the branch that matters most had no test: exercising a failed refund needed a database. Moved to lib/grade-refund.ts (the file that already uses the injectable-deps pattern) as refundReservedSnap(userId, io) with the default io doing exactly what the handler did before. 7 behavioural cases covering the two failure shapes that the ORIGINAL .then(() => {}, () => {}) lost one each of: supabase-js RESOLVES with { error } for a refused write (the empty success callback ate that), and the client can still THROW on a transport failure (the empty rejection callback ate that). Also pinned: it never rejects, because the caller has already decided to answer 502 and a wrapper someone forgets is how the original happened; a non-Error rejection still reports something an operator can act on; and the default io calls refund_snap with the user id, without which every injected case could pass against an io the handler does not use. AN EXISTING GUARD HAD TO FOLLOW THE INDIRECTION: money-path-guards_test.ts read the handler's catch block for captureException(refundErr), which the extraction moved. Weakening it to 'does grade.ts mention refundReservedSnap' would have checked nothing, so it now asserts BOTH halves — the handler still calls the refund in the 502 branch AND the refund still reports both failure shapes — since either alone can hold while the property is gone. MY OWN GUARD ACCUSED ITS OWN COMMENT, third time this session: the assertion that the swallow-everything shape has not returned matched the comment QUOTING it to explain what was wrong. Comments are stripped first now. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED FIVE WAYS: the refused branch going silent, the thrown branch going silent, a refused refund returning true, the handler no longer refunding, and the default io calling the wrong RPC. REMAINING: AC1 for the rest of grade.ts and for admin-billing.ts still needs a request context, a Stripe double and a seeded database — a test HARNESS, unchanged in scope. Both stay declared as MONEY_DEBT. VERIFIED: full edge suite 5384 passed / 0 failed, deno check + lint clean across 1342 files. | 2026-08-03 AC1 ADVANCED for routes/admin-billing.ts — the manual charge-refund path, where an admin sends real money back. No migration. WHAT WAS ALREADY COVERED AND WHAT WAS NOT: the pure decisions were extracted and tested by US-2294 (normalizeRefundAmount, refundIdempotencyKey). Nothing exercised the SEQUENCE — the order of read-charge, validate, create-refund, audit — or any of its failure branches, because the handler drove Stripe and the audit log directly, so reaching a failure meant having a Stripe account that fails on demand. NEW lib/admin-charge-refund.ts holds performAdminChargeRefund + refundableCeiling with injected IO; the route keeps the identical behaviour and now binds Stripe in one adapter. THE PROPERTY THAT MATTERS MOST: a refund that THREW writes NO audit row. A record saying money moved when it did not is worse than no record, because reconciliation trusts this log and the next operator goes looking for a refund that never existed. Also pinned: the audit carries STRIPE quantities rather than the requested ones (a partial Stripe clamped would otherwise be logged at what we asked for), a FULL refund omits the amount field entirely rather than sending 0 (US-2294 bug in its original form — 0 is falsy, the field was dropped, Stripe refunded everything), the idempotency key reaches Stripe, the acting admin is stamped on the Stripe object (the only attribution that survives outside our database), an unreadable charge produces NO refund attempt (the ceiling comes from that read, so proceeding means refunding an unbounded amount), the ceiling is what is LEFT rather than the original amount, and null charge totals yield a zero ceiling rather than NaN. 10 cases. ONE OF MY OWN ASSERTIONS WAS WRONG AND FAILED IMMEDIATELY: it forbade stripe.refunds.create in the handler and fired on my own IO adapter, which is the one legitimate binding. A guard that cannot tell the binding from a bypass would have been deleted by the next reader; it now requires EXACTLY ONE such call and that it sit inside the adapter, which is the real property. COVERAGE FLOOR MOVED WITH IT, per the floor header rule: lib/admin-charge-refund.ts measured 97.9% line, floored at 97. routes/admin-billing.ts STAYS in MONEY_DEBT — the test reads it as TEXT and imports only the new lib, so the route file itself still has zero coverage and the debt entry is still honest. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED SEVEN WAYS: a failed refund writing an audit row, the audit recording our number instead of Stripe s, a full refund sending amount 0, the idempotency key dropped, the ceiling ignoring prior refunds, the admin id no longer stamped, and the route gaining a second direct Stripe path. Each reddened. REMAINING: the rest of grade.ts and admin-billing.ts still want a request-context + Stripe-double harness, unchanged in scope. VERIFIED: full edge suite 5410 passed / 0 failed, deno check + lint clean across 1347 files, coverage floor green at the new numbers.

userStories.title: Impersonation is unbounded, unmarked, non-revocable, and allows account deletion as the user
userStories.description: admin-impersonation.ts:43-132 gets the entry right: super_admin only (:44), users:role scope (:38), fresh step-up (:49), self and privileged targets refused (:54, :68-73), start audited (:116). Everything after the token is minted is open. No time limit — generateLink type magiclink (:90) yields a normal Supabase session for the target, access token plus long-lived refresh token, in the admin's browser, with no cap anywhere. No revocation on stop — src/lib/impersonation.ts:126-129 only redeems the resume token and never calls auth.admin.signOut(targetId), so a copied refresh token outlives the session. No marker — there is no impersonated_by claim and no server-side active-impersonation row, so every request made while impersonating is indistinguishable from the real user's. And destructive actions are fully available: POST /api/account/delete's only server-side control is the confirm string (account.ts:390); the password re-auth at :625-631 is client-side only. A super_admin can impersonate a disputing customer, cancel their subscription and delete their account, and every downstream record shows the customer did it.
acceptanceCriteria: A hard maximum impersonation duration, enforced server-side.
Stopping impersonation revokes the target's sessions.

The impersonated session carries a server-visible marker, and destructive routes (account delete, subscription cancel, marketplace disconnect, grading spend) refuse or require additional authorization while it is set.
The account-delete password re-auth moves server-side.
PRIVILEGED_ROLES (:40) is {admin, super_admin} so a reviewer can be impersonated — decide whether that is intended.
admin-impersonation.ts:137 writes target_id straight from the request body with no check against the start record, so the stop audit row is client-controlled. Fix.
Confirm the GoTrue OTP TTL in prod — it sets the real lifetime of the impersonation and resume tokens.
userStories.notes: [P0][Admin/Security] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. A target's own MFA does not protect them: a magiclink redemption yields an aal1 session. | PARTIAL 2026-08-03 — AC1-AC6 DONE. AC7 is an operator check on prod and stays open. EVERY CLAIM VERIFIED. The entry really is well guarded and the story says so; everything after the token was minted really was open. Confirmed line by line: no cap anywhere, /stop only redeemed the admin's resume token, no marker of any kind, and the stop audit row read target_id straight from the request body. AC1 DONE. NEW admin_impersonation_sessions (00521) plus lib/impersonation-session.ts. Cap is 30 minutes, ENFORCED ON READ rather than by a scheduled sweep — the window between a cap passing and a job noticing is exactly when a forgotten session is most dangerous. And a start that cannot be RECORDED does not happen: a failed insert returns 500 and mints nothing, because a session with no row is precisely the unbounded, unmarked, unrevocable one this story removes. AC2 DONE. /stop revokes the target's sessions through GoTrue's admin logout with scope global. supabase-js cannot do this — auth.admin.signOut wants a JWT, which is the one thing the server does not have — and 'global' is the only scope that reaches a refresh token already copied out of the browser. The result is RETURNED rather than swallowed: an un-revoked stop means the target's tokens are still live and the operator needs to know now. AC3 DONE. The marker is a database row, not a token claim, deliberately: a claim is equally invisible to any route that does not parse it and cannot be revoked once minted. isImpersonated FAILS CLOSED — a lookup error returns true, so a database blip refuses the destructive action. Being wrong that way costs a real user one retry; being wrong the other way is unrecoverable. Guarded by ENUMERATION at eight sites (account delete, buyer + flipdesk subscription cancel, billing portal, and all five marketplace disconnects) rather than by a blanket middleware, which would have to enumerate what is destructive anyway and would silently permit anything it did not know about — the same failure shape US-2354 removed from the scope guard. AC4 DONE. The delete password re-auth moves into the edge, against GoTrue's password grant, and fails CLOSED: an unreachable auth service means the password cannot be proved, and 'cannot prove' must not read as 'proved' on the one endpoint that permanently destroys an account. It deliberately does NOT use the service-role client, which would mint a session — a successful check must prove the password and produce nothing reusable. The browser's local check is REMOVED rather than kept alongside: two places deciding the same thing is how one drifts, and the browser's answer was never the one that mattered. OAuth accounts are exempt on both sides; demanding a password that does not exist is not a control. AC5 DECIDED: reviewer joins PRIVILEGED_ROLES. The set means 'roles whose account carries authority a super_admin should not be able to borrow', not 'roles above a line in the ladder'. A reviewer holds grading:review — they adjust issued grades, which are the product, and RLS grants them human_reviews through is_reviewer_or_admin(). Impersonating one produces a grade adjustment audited to the reviewer rather than to the admin who made it: the same non-repudiation loss the admin exclusion exists to prevent. AC6 DONE: the stop record comes from the START row. The old shape let an admin impersonate one person and log having stopped impersonating another, which is worse than no row because it reads as evidence. A stop with no live session is still audited, with no_active_session set — a double-click and a probe both look like that, and both are worth seeing. PROVEN ON A REAL DATABASE: corpus applied to a throwaway stack, then the target cannot SELECT the row, cannot UPDATE it to end their own impersonation record (0 rows), and the record survives deleting BOTH parties with the emails intact. That last one matters — the record of an impersonation is not the impersonator's to erase. TWO GUARDS CAUGHT MY NEW CODE, both correctly. rls-guard demanded the new table be classified in SERVICE_ROLE_ONLY (deny-all in both directions: a readable table leaks operator activity to the person being impersonated, a writable one lets them end the RECORD while the session continues). no-bare-fetch caught both new outbound calls having no deadline — the GoTrue logout runs while an admin waits on /stop, and the password check is the last thing between a request and a permanent deletion. Both go through fetchWithTimeout now. COLUMN NAMING, worth recording: actor_id / target_id rather than actor_user_id / target_user_id, because rls-guard discovers tenant tables by the literal string user_id and this is an operator table that must have no policy at all. Added to the service-role-tables note as a worked example — the existing rule covers ONE owner column and says to call it owner_user_id, which does not help when there are two. A MISTAKE THAT KEEPS RECURRING, so it is written down: my first AC4 assertion searched for the word signInWithPassword and fired on my own comment explaining what the old local check used to do. Second time this session a guard has accused its own prose. It matches a CALL now. NEW services/edge-functions/src/tests/impersonation-bounds_test.ts, 10 cases. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED THREE WAYS (stop reading the body again, isImpersonated failing open, the guard dropped from one marketplace route), each restored. Vault: NEW vault/20-domain/impersonation.md carries the contract. REMAINING: AC7 — confirm the GoTrue OTP TTL in prod. It sets the real lifetime of the minted impersonation and resume tokens, so it is a SECOND clock running alongside the 30-minute cap: the cap bounds what the server honours, the TTL bounds how long the link stays redeemable. Both should be known. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1317 files, edge suite 5206 passed / 0 failed, web 3225 passed / 0 failed, tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, build green through the 216-route prerender, vault-lint 135 notes clean. | 2026-08-03 FOLLOW-UP on AC5. The decision landed but its REFUSAL MESSAGE did not: adding reviewer to PRIVILEGED_ROLES left the 403 saying "Impersonating an admin or super-admin is not allowed", so a refused reviewer was told about a rule that was not the one applied. That is not cosmetic — the next operator reads a message that disagrees with the code, concludes the check is broken, and goes hunting a bug that is not there. The message now names all three roles and says WHY (their actions audit to them, not to you), and the new test asserts it against PRIVILEGED_ROLES itself rather than a fixed string, so the two cannot drift apart again. AND THE GUARD WAS SATISFIED BY ITS OWN PROSE — a new variant of the recurring trap. My first version checked the raw source slice, which includes the explanatory comment above the message, and that comment names every role: reverting to the stale message left the case GREEN, passing on prose about the very bug it was written to catch. Only the negative verification found it; the assertion read as correct. It strips comments now. Previous instances of this family accused their own prose; this one was SATISFIED by it, which is the more dangerous direction because nothing fails. AC7 remains and is an OPERATOR/CONFIG check, not a database one: the GoTrue OTP TTL is an env var on the self-hosted auth container (GOTRUE_MAILER_OTP_EXP), so it cannot be added to prod-diagnostics.sql. It matters because it is a SECOND clock — the 30-minute cap bounds what the server honours, the TTL bounds how long the minted link stays redeemable, and the longer of the two is the real exposure. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1338 files, full edge suite 5332 passed / 0 failed.

userStories.title: The admin scope drift-guard cannot catch an unguarded mutation, and one already shipped
userStories.description: admin-scope-coverage_test.ts:50 computes hasGuard as src.includes('requireScope('), so a single occurrence anywhere in the file satisfies mode 'mutations'. Router mode correctly asserts the use('*') shape (:81-83), but admin-users.ts, admin-bulk.ts, admin-scopes.ts and admin-guarantee-pool.ts are all mutations mode, so a new unguarded .post() in any of them passes CI. This has already happened: admin-bulk.ts:199 POST /resolve has no requireScope at all and adminBulkRoutes has no router-wide guard (:38). It resolves up to 200 arbitrary emails to {id, email, full_name, suspended} — a user-enumeration and email-confirmation oracle available to any admin regardless of scope.
acceptanceCriteria: The guard parses per-route rather than doing a whole-file substring match.
admin-bulk.ts:199 gets a scope.
A deliberate no-scope route must be explicitly registered as exempt with a reason, not silently pass.

Note the wider context: the default admin role holds 8 of 9 scopes (rbac-scopes.ts:123-132) and the test actively pins it that way, so scope enforcement is a no-op for a default admin and only becomes a real control once an operator narrows a role. Decide whether that default is right.
userStories.notes: [P1][Admin/Security] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | 2026-08-02 EVERY CLAIM VERIFIED, including the one that matters most — the unguarded route really is there. THE GUARD: admin-scope-coverage_test.ts computes const hasGuard = src.includes("requireScope(") — a whole-FILE substring, exactly as reported. For mode "router" it additionally asserts the use("*") shape, so that mode is sound; for mode "mutations" a single requireScope anywhere in the file satisfies it. THE ROUTE THAT ALREADY SLIPPED THROUGH: admin-bulk.ts declares adminBulkRoutes = new Hono<AdminEnv>() with no router-wide use("*"), and its four POSTs are /credits with requireScope("billing:write"), /suspend with requireScope("moderation:write"), /regrade with requireScope("grading:review") — and /resolve with NOTHING. The file passes CI because the other three routes contain the substring. Confirmed what /resolve returns: it accepts up to MAX_TARGETS = 200 entries and answers with {id, email, full_name, suspended} per match, resolved by id OR by email. So it is precisely a user-enumeration and email-confirmation oracle, available to any admin regardless of scope. AC4's CONTEXT CONFIRMED AND EXACT: SCOPE_KEYS lists nine scopes (billing:write, grading:review, moderation:write, content:publish, users:role, ops:write, marketplace:write, support:write, growth:write) and DEFAULT_ROLE_SCOPES.admin lists eight — every one except users:role. So the story's "8 of 9" is right to the key, and the consequence is worth stating plainly: for a DEFAULT admin, every requireScope call in the codebase except users:role is a no-op. Scope enforcement only becomes a real control after an operator narrows a role, and nothing in the product prompts them to. That makes AC4 the highest-leverage AC here — fixing the guard and adding a scope to /resolve hardens a boundary that, for the default configuration, still admits everyone. IMPLEMENTATION NOTE for AC1: "parse per-route" is more than a regex tweak, because the two shapes are different — a router-wide use("*", requireScope(...)) protects everything after it, while a per-route guard sits as the second argument of .get/.post/.patch/.delete. A parser has to recognise both or it will report false positives on every correctly-guarded router-mode file. The nearest existing model in this repo is the enumeration style used by admin-direct-write-guard.test.ts and items-full-bounded-reads.test.ts: enumerate every route with its guard, and require an explicit DECLARED entry with a reason for any that has none — which is also exactly what AC3 asks for. Note both of those guards were reworked on 2026-08-02 under US-2383 (memoized scan + SCAN_TIMEOUT_MS); copy the fixed shape, not the old one, or the new guard becomes the next flake. | 2026-08-02 AC1 AND AC3 SHIPPED. AC2 DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, and the story's framing of it is WRONG — correcting that is the most important part of this note. THE CORRECTION: the story says POST /resolve slipping through is something that "has already happened", implying an accidental omission the weak guard failed to catch. It was not accidental. lib/admin-scope-map.ts's entry for admin-bulk.ts has always carried the rationale "Each bulk op maps to its owning scope: /credits → billing:write, /suspend → moderation:write, /regrade → grading:review. POST /resolve is a read-only target lookup (no scope; US-1562)." So the exemption was a considered, written decision recorded in the very registry the guard reads. The guard's weakness is real and worth fixing; the claim that it let an accident through is not. That distinction matters because AC2 as written ("admin-bulk.ts:199 gets a scope") is a request to REVERSE a prior decision, not to fix a defect — and doing that silently, from a story that mis-describes how the route got there, is how a considered choice gets undone by someone who never saw the argument. AC1 DONE: "mutations" mode is no longer a whole-file src.includes("requireScope(") check. A new ROUTE_REG parses each mutating registration with a 300-char window (so middleware on a following line still counts) and every one must carry its own requireScope. MEASURED before building it: across all four mutations-mode routers — admin-guarantee-pool, admin-users, admin-scopes, admin-bulk — there are 10 mutating routes and exactly ONE without a scope, POST /resolve. So the change reddens nothing except the known case, which is why it could land as an enforcement rather than a migration. AC3 DONE: NEW ADMIN_ROUTE_SCOPE_EXEMPTIONS in admin-scope-map.ts — file + method + path + a mandatory written reason, enforced at 80 characters so "legacy" cannot be the whole justification. /resolve is registered there with the US-1562 argument stated in full AND the counter-argument from this story stated next to it (the response confirms whether an address has an account, so an admin narrowed to no scopes can still enumerate users; reversing it needs a new read scope, since all three bulk ops would want it). The decision is now data a reviewer can argue with instead of prose inside a rationale string. THE EXEMPTION LIST CANNOT ROT: two further tests make it shrink-only — an entry whose route no longer exists fails, and an entry whose route has SINCE been guarded fails and tells you to delete it, so the allowlist can never be what is permitting a route that the guard would now pass on its own. A third test feeds the parser a known sample (guarded, unguarded, and a multi-line registration) and asserts what it sees, because a regex that silently matches nothing would make the whole guard pass vacuously — the same failure as the substring check, one level down. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, not assumed: a probe route added to admin-users.ts made the guard fail naming POST /__probe_unguarded, and repointing /resolve's exemption at a non-existent path made the staleness test fail with the right message. Both probes reverted, tree confirmed clean. VERIFIED: full edge suite 5042 passed / 0 failed, deno lint clean across 1287 files, deno check clean. AC4 REMAINS OPEN and is still the highest-leverage item: nine scopes exist and the default admin holds eight, so for a default admin every requireScope except users:role is a no-op. Hardening route coverage does not change that; deciding whether the default is right does.

userStories.title: Buyer plan gating is never enforced: requireBuyerFeature has zero callers
userStories.description: lib/buyer-entitlements.ts:221 defines requireBuyerFeature, the 402 upgrade-required guard, and nothing calls it. Its helper buyerFeatureEnabled is used only by it and by tests. So no buyer route enforces plan gating except buyer-authenticity.ts:24, which does its own inline check. buyer-wants.ts — the demand board, a Connoisseur-tier feature — has no gate at all. Every buyer paid feature is available on the free tier.
acceptanceCriteria: Inventory which buyer routes are supposed to be tier-gated, and against which tier.
requireBuyerFeature is applied to each of them.
A test asserts every tier-gated buyer route returns 402 for a free-tier user.
Measure how many free-tier buyers have been using paid features before deciding whether to grandfather them.
userStories.notes: [P1][Buyer/Billing] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. The dead-code sweep called this its top finding. Revenue leak, not just dead code. | 2026-08-02 VERIFIED, and quantified. requireBuyerFeature is defined at lib/buyer-entitlements.ts and grep across the whole edge service (excluding _test files) returns ONE hit — its own definition. Zero callers, exactly as reported. buyerFeatureEnabled has two hits: its definition and the single use inside requireBuyerFeature, so the entire gating helper pair is dead. THE SIZE OF THE GAP: BuyerGateFlags in lib/buyer-plans.ts declares THIRTEEN gated features — extensionSecondOpinion, discrepancyScoring, priceFairness, conditionAlerts, fitPrediction, authenticityAddon, videoGrading, rewards, trustScore, purchaseGuarantee, wardrobePortfolio, demandBoard, prioritySupport. Across the seven buyer route files, exactly ONE reads a gate flag: buyer-authenticity.ts checks ent.gateFlags.authenticityAddon inline. buyer-closet.ts, buyer-purchases.ts, buyer-rewards.ts, buyer-trust.ts and buyer-wants.ts contain no gate reference at all (buyer-profile.ts's only hit is the word "entitlements" in a comment). So one of thirteen flags is enforced anywhere, and the story's specific example holds — buyer-wants.ts, the demand board, has no gate. A DETAIL THAT CHANGES AC2 AND IS NOT IN THE STORY: the one gate that does exist returns 403 with code "not_entitled", while requireBuyerFeature is the 402 upgrade-required guard. They are not interchangeable. Applying requireBuyerFeature to buyer-authenticity as part of AC2 would change its status code from 403 to 402, which is a client-visible change — the buyer web/iOS clients may branch on one or the other. Either check the clients first, or leave authenticity on 403 and say why. Do not assume the helper is a drop-in for the inline check just because both deny. SEQUENCING NOTE on AC4: it asks how many free-tier buyers have been using paid features before deciding whether to grandfather. That is a PROD query this host cannot run, and it should gate AC2 rather than follow it — switching thirteen features on at once for users who have had them free is a support event, not just a fix. Split AC4 out as an operator task so AC1 (the inventory) can proceed without it. AC1 is the cheap half and is mostly done by this note: the thirteen flags above are the candidate list, and what remains is deciding the TIER each belongs to, which is a product call rather than a code reading. | PARTIAL 2026-08-03 — AC1, AC2 and AC3 DONE. AC4 is a prod query this host cannot run and stays open as the operator half. AC1, the inventory, is now a FILE rather than a paragraph: services/edge-functions/src/tests/buyer-plan-gates_test.ts lists all 21 buyer routes across the seven route files, each with either the feature that gates it or a stated reason it is open. AC2: TWO ROUTES WERE GENUINELY UNPROTECTED and are now gated. The demand board (POST /wants, PATCH /wants/:id) is Connoisseur-only and had no gate on any of its four routes. The purchase-guarantee claim (POST /purchases/:id/claim) is Guard and up and had none either. Both now call requireBuyerFeature and RETURN its refusal. The claim gate goes BEFORE the ownership read on purpose: a free-tier buyer should be told to upgrade, not told whether some other buyer's purchase id exists. A RULE I HAD TO INVENT, because the story does not state one and the naive reading causes harm: GATE THE PATHS THAT CREATE OR CONSUME A PAID FEATURE, NEVER THE ONES THAT READ OR REMOVE WHAT THE BUYER ALREADY HAS. Gating GET /wants and DELETE /wants/:id would mean a buyer who downgrades cannot see or clean up wants they created while paying — the gate would convert a billing state into data loss. Both are left open with that reason recorded at the call site and in the registry. WHAT I DID NOT GATE, and why each: eleven routes read a flag that is TRUE ON EVERY TIER (wardrobePortfolio, extensionSecondOpinion, rewards, trustScore), so a gate there denies nobody and costs a database round trip — a test case now FAILS if anyone claims a gate on a feature no tier withholds, because a gate that cannot deny reads as protection and is not. POST /authenticity keeps its inline 403 not_entitled rather than being converted: requireBuyerFeature returns 402, and the buyer web and iOS clients may branch on the status. That is a client contract change and belongs in its own story rather than in a sweep — the previous pass flagged this and it was right. AC3: the story asks for a live 402 assertion for a free-tier user. That needs an authenticated request against a seeded buyer, i.e. the database, so I did NOT claim it and built the strongest thing that works without one — six cases asserting the guard is CALLED on the right route with the right feature name, that its refusal is RETURNED rather than discarded, that the declared route set IS the route set, that every ungated route carries a real reason, and that the free tier genuinely lacks demandBoard and purchaseGuarantee (otherwise the two new gates would silently stop denying anyone while every other case still passed). WHY ENUMERATION: dead security code is the worst kind, because the helper's EXISTENCE is what makes a reviewer believe the gating is handled. Nothing about reading buyer-wants.ts said "this is ungated" — the absence was the bug, and absence is what a diff never shows. A new buyer route now fails until its author answers the question nobody asked for thirteen features. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED FOUR WAYS: removed the demand-board gate (reddened naming the route and flag), kept the call but discarded its Response (reddened on the return), added an undeclared /probe route (reddened as an unlisted route), and re-declared the claim gate against the rewards flag (reddened as a gate that denies nobody). Each restored. A MISTAKE WORTH RECORDING: my first route regex was a bare .get( / .post(, which also matched c.get("userId") in every handler and reported a phantom route per file. Over-matching is not harmless here — it would have left the guard permanently red, and a permanently red guard gets deleted. It is anchored to the Routes receiver now and says so. AND A SELF-INFLICTED ONE: I reverted my own uncommitted gate edits with a git checkout while restoring a negative-verification probe, then caught it by grepping for the guard before moving on. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1310 files, full edge suite 5166 passed / 0 failed, tenant-isolation 17/0. REMAINING: AC4 (how many free-tier buyers have been using the demand board and the guarantee claim, to decide grandfathering) is a prod query — it belongs with the other operator diagnostics in scripts/prod-diagnostics.sql. Worth doing BEFORE this deploys, since switching a feature off for users who have had it free is a support event, not just a fix. | 2026-08-03: this story's last open AC is now answerable by scripts/prod-diagnostics.sql, which the operator runs in ONE psql session alongside the other blocked stories. Read-only, verified by executing against a real database with ON_ERROR_STOP=1 — so it cannot fail the operator's session on a wrong column name, which is the failure mode that makes someone distrust the whole file. §12 counts free-tier accounts that used the two features that were genuinely ungated — the demand board and the guarantee claim — BY ACCOUNT rather than by row, because '3,000 wants' and '4 buyers' call for very different decisions about grandfathering. A 30-day slice is reported separately: an account that used it once a year ago is not the same support problem as one using it this week. | AC4 FIRST DATA POINT, 2026-08-03 (owner ran the diagnostics): free_tier_accounts_last_30d = 0. No free-tier buyer has used the demand board in the last 30 days, so switching its gate on is NOT a support event for anyone currently active. That is the half of AC4 that decides urgency. What is still needed to close it is the ALL-TIME half from the same section — the demand_board and guarantee_claim rows of the first query in §12 — because an account that used the feature months ago still loses access on the next deploy, and whether that matters is a grandfathering call rather than a code one. | PROD ANSWER 2026-08-03 (owner ran scripts/prod-diagnostics-console.sql). §12's 30-day slice returned 0. Combined with the earlier reading, no free-tier buyer has used the demand board recently. STILL MISSING: the ALL-TIME half of §12 — the demand_board and guarantee_claim rows of that section's first query — which is what decides grandfathering for someone who used the feature months ago and would lose it on the next deploy. | 2026-08-04 RE-CHECKED — the title is now FALSE and should not be quoted. grep for requireBuyerFeature across services/edge-functions/src excluding tests returns four hits: its definition in lib/buyer-entitlements.ts plus three real call sites — buyer-purchases.ts:301 gating purchaseGuarantee, and buyer-wants.ts:40 and :91 gating demandBoard. Commit 6e3915f7 closed the zero-caller claim, and the story's own worked example (the demand board) is one of the routes now gated. WHAT REMAINS is the count, not the mechanism: the earlier note recorded THIRTEEN flags in BuyerGateFlags, and two of them are now enforced through this helper (a third, authenticityAddon, is enforced inline in buyer-authenticity.ts). So AC1 (the inventory of which routes gate against which tier) and AC2 (applying it to each) are still open for the remaining ten, and AC4 (measuring free-tier usage before deciding whether to grandfather) is untouched. Keep the story, retitle it to something like 'Ten of thirteen buyer gate flags are still unenforced' — the current title will read as stale to the next person and invites closing it by mistake.

userStories.title: No client-side experiment is actually running: useFeatureFlag has zero callers
userStories.description: src/hooks/use-feature-flag.ts:31 is the whole US-2109 PostHog experiment binding and nothing calls it. Any experiment believed to be running on the client is not.
acceptanceCriteria: Confirm against PostHog which experiments are believed to be live.
Either wire the hook into the surfaces that need it, or delete it and close US-2109 with the reason.
If experiments matter, add a check that a flag defined in PostHog with no client consumer is reported.
userStories.notes: [P2][Web/Growth] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. DECISION-then-build. | 2026-08-02 VERIFIED. useFeatureFlag in src/hooks/use-feature-flag.ts has exactly one grep hit across all of src — its own export. Zero callers, so no client-side experiment binding is reachable, and any experiment believed to be running on the web client is not running. The claim is true as stated. WHAT I CANNOT ANSWER, and it is AC1: whether anything is actually configured in PostHog. That needs the PostHog dashboard, not the repo, so AC1 is an operator/owner check and should be split out — AC2's decision (wire it up vs delete it and close US-2109 with the reason) depends entirely on the answer, and the code alone cannot supply it. NOTE ON AC3, because it is the one that would prevent a recurrence and is also the hardest: "a flag defined in PostHog with no client consumer is reported" cannot be a source-scan guard, since one side of the comparison lives in PostHog. It needs either a build-time fetch of the flag list or a periodic job — the cron fleet already has the shape for the latter (see CRON_REGISTRY), and US-2312 (2026-08-02) means such a job's failures would now actually surface rather than reading green. If AC3 is judged too costly, say so and drop it explicitly rather than leaving it open — a half-built experiment framework that nobody can tell is half-built is the exact condition this story documents. | 2026-08-04 RE-CHECKED and the claim STILL HOLDS, unchanged. grep for useFeatureFlag across all of src returns exactly one hit — the export in src/hooks/use-feature-flag.ts:31. Zero callers, same as the 2026-08-02 verification. Commit 98268099 verified this story alongside US-2359 and US-2360, and unlike those two nothing has been wired since. Recording the re-check so the story is not assumed stale by association with its two siblings, which HAVE moved.

userStories.title: Finish the PLANS deprecation: two live callers remain
userStories.description: src/lib/constants.ts:646 PLANS is marked @deprecated with removal blocked on US-211 and US-220, but src/components/admin/platform-analytics.tsx:4 and src/components/flipdesk/bulk-ai-enrich-dialog.tsx:23 still import it.
acceptanceCriteria: Both callers migrate to the current source.
PLANS is removed and the blocking stories are updated.
Separately: 85 exports in src/ are exported but used only inside their own file — dropping the export keyword is safe and shrinks the public surface. Batch it with this.
userStories.notes: [P3][Web/Cleanup] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | AC1 and AC2 DONE 2026-08-03. AC3 (the 85 file-local exports) is NOT done and is argued against below rather than deferred silently. THE STORY SAID TWO CALLERS. THERE WERE SIX, across 15 call sites: platform-analytics.tsx and bulk-ai-enrich-dialog.tsx as reported, plus dashboard.tsx, settings.tsx, admin/users.tsx and admin/user-detail.tsx (10 sites on its own). Worth stating because the story's count is what made this look like a five-minute job, and because the extras accumulated precisely BECAUSE the alias made the legacy dependency invisible. THE FINDING THAT SHAPED THE FIX: the legacy vocabulary is NOT dead code. public.user_plan ('free'|'starter'|'professional'|'enterprise') is still the type of the users.plan COLUMN, and the admin dashboard's planDistribution is GROUPED BY IT in SQL (00513). So a caller reading that column genuinely has to translate — the mistake was hiding the translation inside a deprecated alias, where it read as legacy cruft nobody depended on. So PLANS is gone and the translation is explicit: NEW flipdeskPlanForLegacy() and legacyPlanConfig() in constants.ts, both named and non-deprecated. Callers that hold a legacy value can now be SEEN doing so. legacyPlanConfig is deliberately tolerant (returns undefined for an unknown string) because every call site reads straight off a user row and already guarded with ?. — an unrecognised plan must degrade to showing the raw value, not throw on an admin page. Where the profile carries flipdesk_plan, callers now prefer it and fall back to translating — settings.tsx already had that shape and it is now the pattern everywhere, rather than one file doing it right. TWO FIELD RENAMES THE SHIM WAS PAPERING OVER, and both are places a careless migration would have shipped a wrong number: priceMonthly was DOLLARS (the shim divided by 100) against priceMonthlyCents on the source, and gradesPerMonth was includedStandardGradesPerMonth. The conversions are now visible at the two sites that need them. The shim's null 'Custom' price branch is also gone — no current tier carries a null price, so it was a branch that could not fire. AC3 NOT DONE, AND I AM RECOMMENDING AGAINST BATCHING IT HERE. 'Drop the export keyword on 85 symbols used only in their own file' is a different change with a different risk profile: it touches 85 files for no behavioural reason, it conflicts with anything else in flight (a concurrent agent is editing this tree today), and 'used only in its own file' is a fact about the CURRENT tree that a test file or a future import invalidates — several of those exports are almost certainly exported so a test can reach them, and un-exporting those breaks the test rather than shrinking the surface. It wants its own pass with the test importers excluded from the count first. Batching a mechanical 85-file sweep onto a semantic 6-file migration would also make the semantic change unreviewable, which is the more expensive of the two. ALSO FOUND, not fixed, and worth its own look: the admin revenue chart computes MRR from users.plan — the DEPRECATED column — not from flipdesk_plan. 00039 backfilled the two once and nothing keeps them in step, so if they ever diverge the admin's revenue number is computed from the stale one. That is a correctness question about the dashboard rather than about this deprecation, which is why it is recorded rather than swept in here. VERIFIED: tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, 260 files / 3236 tests 0 failed, build green through the 216-route prerender, bundle budget OK, impeccable clean on the two largest touched pages. | AC3 MEASURED 2026-08-03, and the measurement is the deliverable: the AC as written should be dropped or re-scoped, not executed. NEW scripts/audit-file-local-exports.mjs is the reproducible report. THE COUNT IS NOT 85. It is 936 — 629 types/interfaces and 307 runtime values. An estimate off by an order of magnitude is not a scoping error; it changes what the task is. A single commit dropping 936 export keywords is unreviewable and conflicts with everything else in flight. AND 230 MORE ARE IMPORTED ONLY BY TESTS — a group by itself nearly three times the story's entire claimed total. Those are not dead surface: they are exported so a test can reach them, and un-exporting one BREAKS THE TEST rather than shrinking anything. The previous pass predicted exactly this and made excluding them the precondition for doing the work; the numbers say the precondition was the whole story. 'SAFE' ALSO FAILS ON WHERE THEY LIVE, which is the part a count alone hides. 162 sit in src/types/database.ts — the app's type vocabulary, where an unused row type is a description of a table that exists rather than clutter. 52 are hooks in use-ebay.ts and 31 are constants: an exported hook nobody calls is DEAD CODE, and the honest answer there is wire-it-or-delete-it (US-2362's question), not quietly making it file-private and leaving it running. Dropping the export keyword on those would HIDE the finding instead of resolving it. RECOMMENDATION: amend AC3 to name the one group where the change is both safe and worth doing — never-imported RUNTIME values in component and page files, excluding types/database.ts, the hook modules and constants — or drop it and let US-2362's wire-or-delete pass cover the values. Either way it is a different story from finishing the PLANS deprecation, which is what AC1/AC2 did and what this story's title is about. The report separates the three groups (--list, --tests) so whoever decides is reading numbers rather than an estimate. | ⚠ CORRECTION 2026-08-03 to this story's own 'ALSO FOUND' note, which was WRONG. It said 'the admin revenue chart computes MRR from users.plan — the DEPRECATED column — not from flipdesk_plan'. It does not. 00215_revenue_dashboard.sql prices MRR by joining pricing_plans on u.flipdesk_plan and never touches the legacy column. I went to act on that note, re-verified first, and found it did not hold — the same discipline this session has been applying to audit claims, applied to my own. THE REAL DEFECT IS ADJACENT AND LARGER, and is now FILED AS US-2398. Nothing has written users.plan since the 00039 backfill (no .update({ plan: … }) in the edge, no SET plan = in any migration), and FOUR admin metrics still read it: totalPaid and churnFreeWithActivity in 00514, planDistribution and topUsers[].plan in 00513. So the headline revenue number is correct while the paid COUNT, the churn estimate and the plan mix beside it on the same dashboard are frozen at 2024 — and the two errors compound in the same direction, which makes the dashboard tell a consistent story about a business doing worse than it is. NEW src/test/legacy-user-plan-readers.test.ts stops a FIFTH reader appearing while US-2398 waits for a migration window — four accumulated because nothing ever objected to the fourth. It also pins that MRR is NOT among them, so the next reader does not repeat the mistake this note is correcting. | 2026-08-04 RE-CHECKED, with a warning for whoever picks this up. The title is now FALSE — AC1/AC2 are done and the deprecated PLANS object is gone from src/lib/constants.ts (line 611 is the tombstone comment explaining what replaced it). BEWARE A FALSE POSITIVE: grep for a bare PLANS token still hits src/pages/admin/monitoring.tsx:155 and :314, but that is an unrelated file-local const PLANS: FlipdeskPlan[] used to render a filter dropdown. It is not the deprecated shim and must not be 'migrated'. Only AC3 is open — the file-local exports — and the previous note already argues that the story's count of 85 is wrong (it is 936, of which 230 must not be touched). Since AC3 is a different piece of work from the thing the title describes, this is a candidate to close and re-file rather than carry.

userStories.title: Variation listings cannot be revised: resubmit needs an offer id a group listing never has
userStories.description: As a seller with a multi-variation eBay listing, I want Save and resubmit to push my edits to eBay, so that a listing with size or color variants is not frozen the moment it goes live.
acceptanceCriteria: POST /api/flipdesk/ebay/listings/:id/revise on a listing whose listings.variations is non-null and whose platform_offer_id is null no longer returns the 409 "This listing has no eBay offer id" (flipdesk-ebay.ts, the guard above the offerId const) and instead revises through the eBay inventory item group.

The revise resolves its strategy group-FIRST, the same way the end path does via resolveEndStrategy (flipdesk-ebay.ts:8836), and keys the group on the PINNED listings.inventory_sku rather than the current inventory_items.sku, so a SKU rename cannot orphan the live group.

The group branch updates every variant inventory item and then calls createOrReplaceInventoryItemGroup and publishOfferByInventoryItemGroup (both already exported from services/edge-functions/src/lib/ebay-client.ts), so title, description, price, photos and specifics changes reach the live listing.

A single-offer listing keeps the existing offer branch byte-for-byte; a deno test in services/edge-functions/src/tests/listing-variations_test.ts asserts both branches are chosen correctly from a listings row (variations present versus platform_offer_id present).

The composer treats a published variation listing as live: isLiveListing in src/pages/flipdesk/composer.tsx stops requiring platform_offer_id when listings.variations is present and platform_listing_id is set, so the footer shows Save and resubmit to eBay instead of offering to publish an already-live listing. A vitest guard pins that gate.

Tenant scoping is unchanged: the revise route still reaches the listing through an owner-verified parent row (US-268), and services/edge-functions/src/tests/tenant-isolation_test.ts gains a case covering the group-revise branch.

Verified after deploy against a real multi-variation listing, not by reading code: the publish path never writes platform_offer_id for a group (the variation listingPayload in flipdesk-ebay.ts omits it), so unit tests alone cannot prove the round trip.
userStories.notes: PARTIAL 2026-08-03 — AC2, AC4 and AC5 DONE, plus a truthful refusal in place of misleading advice. AC1, AC3, AC6 and AC7 remain, and the reason is scoped rather than vague. VERIFIED THE WHOLE CHAIN FIRST. The revise route really does begin with `if (!row.listing.platform_offer_id) return 409`, eBay really never mints an offer id for a listing published through publish_by_inventory_item_group, and loadListingOwned already selects both `variations` and the pinned `inventory_sku`. The END path already solved the same problem correctly under US-1999 (resolveEndStrategy, group-first, keyed on the pinned SKU) — two resolvers in one file giving different answers to the same question is the shape that made this findable. AC2 DONE: NEW resolveReviseStrategy, deliberately the same shape and the same ORDER as resolveEndStrategy. Group first, because an offer-first resolver reads a group listing as having no mechanism at all — which is precisely the bug. Keyed on the PINNED listings.inventory_sku, since the inventory_item_group was created under the base SKU at publish and a later rename would aim the revise at a group that does not exist. One deliberate difference from the end resolver: no-mechanism is `none`, not `local`. Ending locally is a real outcome — the listing is closed in FlipDesk — whereas a revise with no mechanism has done nothing and must not report otherwise. A test pins both the agreement and that single divergence. AC5 DONE, AND IT WAS THE WORSE HALF OF THE BUG. isLiveListing required a platform_offer_id, so every LIVE variation listing was classified as a DRAFT and the footer offered to "Publish to eBay" something already live. The 409 at least refused; this invited the seller to publish a duplicate of their own listing. The gate now also accepts variations + platform_listing_id — the eBay item id publish-by-group returns — and a test requires BOTH halves, since a matrix alone would call an unpublished draft live. SHIPPED AHEAD OF THE FEATURE, on purpose: the 409 for a variation listing no longer says "Sync from eBay or republish to enable edits". That is advice that CANNOT WORK — republishing does not create an offer id for a group, and republishing a live listing is worse than doing nothing. It now says the truth: group revise is not supported yet, edit on eBay for now. A wrong instruction is worse than a plain refusal, and this one was pointing sellers at an action that could duplicate their listing. AC4 DONE: seven cases appended to listing-variations_test.ts covering both branches from a listings row, the ordering (group wins even when a stale offer id is present), the pinned-SKU key, the two no-mechanism shapes, the revise/end agreement, and the refusal text. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED: the resolver flipped to offer-first (reddened on the ordering case) and the composer's variation branch reduced to the matrix alone (reddened on the both-halves case). WHAT REMAINS AND WHY I DID NOT DO IT. AC1/AC3 are the group-revise branch itself: update every variant inventory item, then createOrReplaceInventoryItemGroup and publishOfferByInventoryItemGroup. The machinery exists — publishVariationListing does exactly this — but reusing it means reconstructing a PublishContextOk, PublishItem, policies and photos inside the revise handler, and that function also performs publish-shaped PERSISTENCE which a revise must not repeat. It is a substantial change to the most sensitive file in the service, on the path every seller's Save-and-resubmit uses, and AC7 states plainly that unit tests cannot prove the round trip because the publish path never writes platform_offer_id for a group. Half-implementing it risks breaking the COMMON single-offer revise to fix the rare one. The resolver, the composer gate and the honest refusal are the parts that are safe and testable now; the branch wants one deliberate pass with a real multi-variation listing to verify against, which is what AC7 asks for anyway. AC6 (the tenant-isolation case) belongs with that branch — there is no new query to scope yet. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1323 files, edge suite 5245 passed / 0 failed, web 260 files / 3236 tests 0 failed, tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, build green through the 216-route prerender.
